summary: Defines a data transfer protocol for moving data between hosts on the ARPANET, written by a group of authors from MIT, UCLA, BBN, Rand, SRI, Harvard and UCSB. It updates RFC 114 and works with the file transfer protocol. It was replaced by RFC 264.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 171 defines a shared mechanism for applications to divide network data into transactions. It provides three transfer modes and several control transaction types.

subtitle: Defines transaction modes for transferring data and control information between ARPANET hosts.

tldr.problem: Many ARPANET applications needed a common low-level way to delimit data blocks and separate data from control information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 171 defines three transaction modes, transaction type codes, and a handshake for exchanging supported transfer modes.
tldr.outcome: It was updated by RFC 238 and obsoleted by RFC 264, which revised the protocol.

today: RFC 171 was updated by RFC 238 and obsoleted by RFC 264.

sections.title: A Low-Level Transfer Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 171 defines a low-level Data Transfer Protocol for file transfer, remote job entry, network mail, graphics, remote execution and block terminals. It separates data transfer from application functions to improve implementation flexibility and reduce the proliferation of programs and protocols.

DTP separates messages into logical blocks, distinguishes data from control information and includes some error-control mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: DTP provides shared rules for how applications delimit and label data. The applications themselves decide what the data means.

sections.title: Three Transaction Modes
sections.content:
The protocol allows an indefinite bit stream that ends when the connection closes, a transparent block that ends at DLE ETX, and a descriptor-and-count mode with separate counts for information and filler bits.

Modes can be mixed on one connection and can carry data or control information. An application may define which modes are workable, and a handshake exchanges information about modes available for sending and receiving.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to mark transaction boundaries: close the connection, send an escape sequence, or provide counts in a descriptor. The application chooses which modes it supports.

sections.title: Types, Separators and Error Messages
sections.content:
Each transaction begins with a type byte. The types identify transfer modes, a modes-available handshake, information separators, error codes, aborts and a no-op.

Separators can mark units, records, groups and files in a hierarchy. Error transactions may identify an error and sequence number, but DTP does not require the receiver to take recovery action. Applications define how aborts are handled.
sections.plainLanguage: Type codes tell the receiver whether a transaction carries data or control information. DTP leaves error recovery to the application protocol.
